Transfer entropy between states

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/transfer-entropy.Rmd
transfer-entropy.Rmd

Transfer entropy (Schreiber, 2000) measures directed predictive coupling: how much knowing the past of a source series XX reduces the uncertainty about the future of a target series YY, over and above what the target’s own past already tells. With Yt+ℓY_{t+\ell} the target ℓ\ell steps ahead, Yt(k)Y_t^{(k)} the target’s last kk values and XtX_t the source’s current value,

TX→Y=H(Yt+ℓ∣Yt(k))−H(Yt+ℓ∣Yt(k),Xt),T_{X \to Y} = H\big(Y_{t+\ell} \mid Y_t^{(k)}\big) - H\big(Y_{t+\ell} \mid Y_t^{(k)}, X_t\big),

measured in bits. It is zero when the source adds nothing to the target’s own history, and it is not symmetric: TX→YT_{X \to Y} and TY→XT_{Y \to X} are separate quantities. Because it conditions on the target’s past, a process with strong momentum does not inflate it the way it inflates a plain lagged association.

Transfer entropy answers a different question from lag sequential analysis. An adjusted residual says whether the transition i→ji \to j occurs more or less often than base rates predict, and its sign says which. Transfer entropy says how much information one series carries about the next step of another, and it has no sign: a source that makes the target’s next state less likely is as informative as one that makes it more likely. The two are read together, as this guide shows. transfer_entropy() is marked experimental in the package.

library(lagdynamics)

Data

  • engagement: weekly engagement states (Active, Average, Disengaged) of 138 students over 15 weeks, one row per student; two rows are entirely missing.
  • group_regulation: coded regulation actions in 2,000 collaborative learning sessions, one row per session and one column per ordered time point (T1 to T26), nine states.
  • ai_long: a long log of 8,551 coded behaviours of an AI coding assistant in 428 “vibe-coding” sessions from 34 projects, in which a person builds software by instructing the assistant in natural language. Each row is one coded behaviour, ordered within its session by order_in_session. The column code holds one of eight behaviour codes (Ask, Delegate, Execute, Explain, Investigate, Plan, Repair, Report) and the column cluster the broader category the code belongs to (Action, Communication, Repair).

The estimator

transfer_entropy() computes plug-in Shannon entropies from pooled (target future, target history, source value) triples. Each sequence contributes the triples that fit inside it, so the lag never crosses from one sequence into the next, and triples with a missing value are dropped. The returned table has one row per ordered pair with the columns:

  • te: the transfer entropy in bits.
  • te_normalised: te divided by the target’s leftover uncertainty H(Yt+ℓ∣Yt(k))H(Y_{t+\ell} \mid Y_t^{(k)}), so it is the share of what the target’s own past leaves unexplained that the source explains (0 to 1).
  • te_effective: te minus the mean transfer entropy of the surrogates, a bias-corrected value (surrogate test only).
  • p: the surrogate p-value (surrogate test only).
  • n: the number of pooled triples.

Rows are ordered by decreasing te. The arguments lag (ℓ\ell, default 1) and history (kk, default 1) set the prediction horizon and the length of the target’s own past.

A state network from one sequence dataset

Given one set of categorical sequences, transfer_entropy() returns a directed network among the states. Each ordered pair of states s→rs \to r is turned into two binary series: the source is “the unit is in ss” and the target is “the unit is in rr”. The transfer entropy of the pair is then the information that being in ss now gives about being in rr next, beyond whether the unit is in rr now. Self-pairs are not computed, so KK states give K(K−1)K(K-1) rows. The call below skips the significance test.

transfer_entropy(engagement, test = "none")
#>         from         to      te te_normalised    n
#> 1     Active Disengaged 0.03645       0.06002 1734
#> 2    Average Disengaged 0.03645       0.06002 1734
#> 3     Active    Average 0.00695       0.00752 1734
#> 4 Disengaged    Average 0.00695       0.00752 1734
#> 5    Average     Active 0.00479       0.00635 1734
#> 6 Disengaged     Active 0.00479       0.00635 1734

The largest flows end in Disengaged: knowing whether a student is Active this week gives 0.036 bits about whether the student is Disengaged next week, 6.0% of the uncertainty that the student’s own disengagement status leaves. Flows into Average and Active are five to eight times smaller (0.007 and 0.005 bits). The rows come in identical pairs. This is a property of the binary decomposition with three states: once the target’s own indicator says the student is not Disengaged, the student is either Active or Average, so the two source indicators carry the same information. The documentation of transfer_entropy() notes this redundancy; with three states the network has three distinct values, one per target, and a larger alphabet or the bivariate mode below is needed for source-specific flows.

Testing against surrogates

A plug-in estimate of transfer entropy is positive even when the source and the target are unrelated, because sampling noise always produces some apparent information. The surrogate test (test = "surrogate", the default) shuffles the source values across the pooled triples R times, which breaks the coupling between source and target while keeping both marginal distributions, and recomputes the transfer entropy each time. The p-value is (1+#{Tsurrogate≥Tobserved})/(R+1)(1 + \#\{T_\text{surrogate} \ge T_\text{observed}\}) / (R + 1), and the effective transfer entropy subtracts the surrogate mean. seed makes the shuffles reproducible.

transfer_entropy(engagement, R = 199, seed = 2026)
#>         from         to      te te_effective te_normalised     p    n
#> 1     Active Disengaged 0.03645      0.03569       0.06002 0.005 1734
#> 2    Average Disengaged 0.03645      0.03559       0.06002 0.005 1734
#> 3     Active    Average 0.00695      0.00607       0.00752 0.005 1734
#> 4 Disengaged    Average 0.00695      0.00613       0.00752 0.005 1734
#> 5    Average     Active 0.00479      0.00396       0.00635 0.010 1734
#> 6 Disengaged     Active 0.00479      0.00397       0.00635 0.010 1734

The four flows into Disengaged and Average exceed all 199 surrogates (p=0.005p = 0.005, the smallest attainable value), and the two flows into Active exceed all but one (p=0.010p = 0.010). The bias correction is small: the effective transfer entropy of Active -> Disengaged is 0.0357 bits against an estimate of 0.0365, because 1,734 triples leave little room for noise. The directed flows are real, and the flow towards disengagement is the one of practical size.

Longer history and longer horizon

The history argument conditions on more of the target’s own past.

transfer_entropy(engagement, history = 2, test = "none")
#>         from         to       te te_normalised    n
#> 1     Active Disengaged 0.033837       0.06105 1603
#> 2    Average Disengaged 0.033837       0.06105 1603
#> 3    Average     Active 0.001273       0.00180 1603
#> 4 Disengaged     Active 0.001273       0.00180 1603
#> 5     Active    Average 0.000938       0.00106 1603
#> 6 Disengaged    Average 0.000938       0.00106 1603

With two weeks of the target’s own status known, the flows into Active and Average shrink to between a quarter and an eighth of their size (from 0.0048 to 0.0013 bits into Active, from 0.0070 to 0.0009 into Average), while the flow into Disengaged barely moves (0.0338 bits). Most of what the current state said about the next active or average week was already contained in the student’s own recent history; what it says about the next disengaged week is not. The lag argument moves the prediction horizon in the same way as in lsa(); lag = 2 asks about the state two weeks ahead.

A larger alphabet

With nine states the binary channels are no longer redundant and each ordered pair carries its own value. The call below lists the strongest flows of the group_regulation network.

regulation_te <- transfer_entropy(group_regulation, test = "none")
head(regulation_te, 8)
#>        from         to     te te_normalised     n
#> 1 consensus       plan 0.0586        0.0751 25533
#> 2   emotion   cohesion 0.0584        0.1648 25533
#> 3   discuss       plan 0.0458        0.0587 25533
#> 4   discuss  synthesis 0.0419        0.2352 25533
#> 5 consensus coregulate 0.0275        0.0677 25533
#> 6      plan coregulate 0.0190        0.0467 25533
#> 7 synthesis      adapt 0.0150        0.1035 25533
#> 8 consensus   cohesion 0.0149        0.0421 25533

The strongest flows run from consensus to plan (0.059 bits) and from emotion to cohesion (0.058 bits). Among these eight flows, discuss -> synthesis has the largest normalised value: it explains 23.5% of the leftover uncertainty about whether the next action is a synthesis, against 7.5% for consensus -> plan. The surrogate test is omitted here: its cost grows with R times the number of ordered pairs, which is 72 for nine states.

The lag sequential analysis of the same data gives the signs.

transitions(lsa(group_regulation), significant = TRUE,
            sort = "strength") |> head(6)
#>        from         to lag count expected   prob prob_col adj_res         p yules_q
#> 1   emotion   cohesion   1   923    190.9 0.3253   0.5373    58.2  0.00e+00   0.860
#> 2   discuss  synthesis   1   557    106.8 0.1410   0.8072    48.0  0.00e+00   0.927
#> 3 synthesis      adapt   1   153     13.6 0.2347   0.2881    38.8  0.00e+00   0.904
#> 4   discuss       plan   1    46    961.6 0.0116   0.0074   -36.9 2.20e-298  -0.943
#> 5 consensus  consensus   1   519   1578.7 0.0820   0.0815   -35.5 5.32e-276  -0.661
#> 6 consensus coregulate   1  1188    519.3 0.1877   0.5671    35.3 3.36e-273   0.647
#>    kappa kappa_z   kappa_p    lift  sign significant
#> 1  0.439    55.0  0.00e+00  4.8353  over        TRUE
#> 2  0.721    46.1  0.00e+00  5.2168  over        TRUE
#> 3  0.256    37.0 2.44e-299 11.2837  over        TRUE
#> 4 -0.955   -38.2 2.88e-319  0.0478 under        TRUE
#> 5 -0.691   -37.6 7.65e-309  0.3287 under        TRUE
#> 6  0.412    34.6 5.06e-262  2.2877  over        TRUE

emotion -> cohesion is a strong flow in both analyses and over-represented (z=58.2z = 58.2): emotional expressions are followed by cohesion. discuss -> plan is the third largest flow of information (0.046 bits) but the most avoided transition of the table (z=−36.9z = -36.9, 46 observed against 962 expected): a discussion predicts that the next action is not planning. Transfer entropy ranks the two among the most informative relations of the network; only the residual says that one is an attraction and the other an avoidance. Read transfer entropy for the strength of directed dependence and the adjusted residual for its direction.

Two aligned series

When y is supplied, transfer_entropy() computes the full-alphabet transfer entropy between two aligned series, in both directions. The two series must have the same shape: the same number of sequences and the same length within each. In ai_long every coded behaviour carries both its code and its cluster, so the two columns are aligned by construction. The log is ordered by session and by position within session, and the columns are passed as one long series each.

with(ai_long, transfer_entropy(code, cluster, R = 199, seed = 2026))
#>      from      to     te te_effective te_normalised     p    n
#> 1    code cluster 0.0715      0.06775        0.0642 0.005 8550
#> 2 cluster    code 0.0000     -0.00981        0.0000 1.000 8550

The coupling is one-directional. The code of the current behaviour carries 0.0715 bits about the cluster of the next one beyond what the current cluster says (p=0.005p = 0.005). The reverse flow is exactly 0: the cluster is a function of the code, so the current cluster cannot tell anything about the next code that the current code does not already tell. The negative effective value (−0.0098-0.0098) is the bias correction applied to a true zero. Passed as one long series, the 8,550 pairs include the 427 that join the last behaviour of one session to the first of the next, about 5% of the total; a series per session (one row per session, NA-padded) avoids them.

Transfer entropy and lag sequential analysis

Lag sequential analysis Transfer entropy
Question Does i→ji \to j occur more or less than base rates predict? How much does the source’s present tell about the target’s future beyond the target’s own past?
Sign Signed: over- or under-represented Unsigned: attraction and avoidance both count
Conditioning On the margins of the transition table On the target’s own history (history)
Unit zz, odds ratio, probability Bits, or a share of leftover uncertainty
Test Normal reference, bootstrap, permutation Source-shuffling surrogates
Function lsa(), transitions() transfer_entropy()

Use lag sequential analysis to name the transitions that occur more or less than expected and to test them. Add transfer entropy when the question is which states carry predictive information about others once each state’s own persistence is accounted for, and when a process has strong momentum, as the engagement data do. Report transfer entropy with the surrogate p-value and next to the signed residual, never on its own.

References

Schreiber, T. (2000). Measuring information transfer. Physical Review Letters, 85(2), 461-464.
